item.title: Buy to let sales outstrip purchases four to one
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent research from Aldermore Bank highlights a significant shift in the buy-to-let property market, with landlords selling rental properties at four times the rate of new purchases. This trend suggests a period of consolidation, where smaller investors are exiting the market while larger portfolio landlords continue to expand their holdings.

Landlords rebalancing property portfolios

The latest figures indicate a notable increase in property sales by buy-to-let investors, with many choosing to divest from the private rental sector. Market analysts suggest several factors may be influencing this trend, including recent tax changes, stricter regulations, and shifting property values across different regions.

Smaller landlords appear to be leading this exodus, often citing increased administrative burdens and reduced profit margins as key reasons for selling up. Meanwhile, professional investors with larger portfolios are taking advantage of market conditions to acquire additional properties, potentially benefiting from economies of scale that smaller operators cannot match.

Market consolidation creates new opportunities

This divergence between small-scale and large-scale landlords is creating a two-tier market. Property professionals note that experienced investors with substantial portfolios are often better positioned to navigate the current regulatory environment and absorb higher operating costs.

For those considering buy-to-let investments, the current market conditions present both challenges and potential opportunities:

  • Regional variations in property prices and rental yields may favour certain locations
  • Mortgage products tailored for portfolio landlords could offer competitive terms
  • Tax planning strategies may help mitigate some of the recent fiscal changes

As the market continues to evolve, prospective investors might wish to seek professional financial advice and conduct thorough research before making any property investment decisions. The changing landscape could potentially reward those with a long-term strategy and sufficient resources to weather current market pressures.

item.title: Rent arrears biggest cause of repossessions
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Recent research from the National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) has highlighted that unpaid rent remains the primary reason landlords seek possession of rental properties. This comes amidst growing concerns over escalating taxes and housing costs, which are putting additional pressure on both tenants and landlords.

The Impact of Rent Arrears

Rent arrears have emerged as a significant issue in the UK rental market, with many landlords facing financial strain due to unpaid rent. According to the NRLA, this is the leading cause of repossessions, as landlords struggle to cover their own costs, including mortgage payments, maintenance, and rising taxes. For tenants, falling behind on rent can lead to eviction proceedings, creating a cycle of financial instability.

Challenges for Landlords

Landlords are finding it increasingly difficult to navigate the financial pressures of the current housing market. Rising taxes, including changes to mortgage interest relief and stamp duty, have added to their financial burdens. Additionally, the cost of maintaining properties and complying with regulatory requirements has increased. These factors, combined with rent arrears, have forced many landlords to consider repossession as a last resort.

  • Financial Strain: Landlords face mounting costs, including mortgage payments and property maintenance.
  • Regulatory Pressures: Compliance with new regulations adds to the financial burden.
  • Tax Changes: Recent tax reforms have reduced profitability for many landlords.

Support for Tenants and Landlords

To address these challenges, both tenants and landlords may benefit from exploring available support options. Tenants struggling to pay rent could seek advice from housing charities or local councils, whilst landlords might consider engaging with tenants early to discuss payment plans or seek mediation services. Government initiatives and support schemes could also play a role in alleviating financial pressures on both parties.

As the rental market continues to evolve, it is essential for both tenants and landlords to stay informed about their rights and responsibilities. By addressing rent arrears proactively and seeking support where needed, it may be possible to reduce the number of repossessions and create a more stable rental environment for all involved.

item.title: Northern landlords face £15,000 tax hit
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Property investors in northern England could face significant financial challenges due to upcoming tax changes, with potential losses of up to £15,000 over a 25-year period, according to recent analysis. These tax adjustments, primarily affecting rental income, may reshape the landscape for landlords across the region.

Impact of Tax Changes on Northern Landlords

The tax reforms, which are set to increase the financial burden on landlords, could have a particularly pronounced effect in northern England. Rathbones, a leading investment management firm, has highlighted that these changes may result in substantial long-term costs for property investors. The estimated £15,000 hit over a quarter of a century underscores the importance of careful financial planning for those relying on rental income.

Why Northern England May Be More Affected

Northern England’s property market has historically offered lower purchase prices compared to the South, making it an attractive option for investors. However, the tax increases could erode the profitability of these investments. Landlords in the region might find themselves disproportionately impacted, as the tax changes could take a larger percentage of their rental income. This could lead to a reassessment of investment strategies, with some landlords potentially reducing their portfolios or increasing rents to offset the additional costs.

What Landlords Can Do

Whilst the tax changes present a challenge, there are steps landlords might consider to mitigate their impact. Reviewing current property portfolios and exploring tax-efficient investment structures could be beneficial. Additionally, landlords may wish to seek professional financial advice to navigate the complexities of the new tax landscape. Staying informed and proactive could help ensure long-term financial stability in the face of these changes.

As the tax reforms come into effect, landlords across northern England will need to adapt to maintain profitability. Understanding the implications and planning accordingly will be crucial in navigating this evolving financial environment.

item.title: London rents rise by £1k
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

London’s rental market has seen significant increases over the past year, with tenants in several boroughs facing annual rent rises exceeding £1,000. According to recent research from Benham and Reeves, the capital’s soaring rental costs highlight the growing financial pressures on renters across the city.

Sharp increases across London boroughs

The data reveals that 11 London boroughs have experienced annual rent hikes of more than £1,000. This upward trend reflects a combination of factors, including high demand for rental properties and limited supply. Boroughs such as Kensington and Chelsea, Westminster, and Camden are among those where tenants are feeling the pinch the most. For many, these increases represent a significant portion of their monthly income, raising concerns about affordability in the capital.

Impact on tenants and the rental market

The rising costs are placing additional strain on tenants, many of whom are already grappling with the high cost of living. With rents climbing steadily, renters may need to reassess their budgets or consider alternative areas to live. Meanwhile, landlords could face challenges in retaining tenants if affordability becomes a persistent issue. This dynamic could lead to shifts in the rental market, with tenants potentially seeking more affordable options in outer boroughs or neighbouring regions.

For those considering renting in London, it could be worth researching rental trends in different boroughs to identify areas that offer better value for money. Additionally, tenants might explore negotiating rent agreements or seeking properties that include utilities to help manage costs.

Looking ahead

As the capital’s rental market continues to evolve, both tenants and landlords will need to navigate the challenges posed by rising costs. Policymakers and industry stakeholders may also need to address the issue of affordability to ensure the rental market remains accessible for all. In the meantime, staying informed about market trends and exploring flexible housing solutions could help renters adapt to the changing landscape.

London’s rental market remains dynamic, but with careful planning and informed decision-making, tenants can better manage the financial pressures of renting in the city.

item.title: Top 5 Edinburgh rental yield hotspots revealed
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New research has highlighted five Edinburgh postcodes that delivered particularly strong rental yields during the third quarter of 2026, offering potential insights for property investors. The findings combine rental data from Citylets with house price analysis from Scottish property portal ESPC.

Edinburgh's top performing rental areas

The analysis reveals that certain neighbourhoods in the Scottish capital continue to offer attractive returns for buy-to-let investors. Whilst rental yields across the UK have faced pressure from rising interest rates and changing market conditions, these Edinburgh locations bucked the trend with above-average performance between July and September 2026.

Property investors might consider that Edinburgh's combination of strong student demand, thriving professional sectors and limited housing supply helps maintain rental yields in certain areas. The city's historic appeal and growing reputation as a tech hub also contribute to its rental market resilience.

What makes a strong rental yield area?

Several factors typically contribute to higher rental yields in specific postcodes:

  • Strong tenant demand relative to available properties
  • Competitive purchase prices compared to rental values
  • Proximity to universities or employment centres
  • Good transport links and local amenities
  • A mix of property types appealing to different tenant groups

Whilst the specific postcodes haven't been detailed in this summary, investors looking at the Edinburgh market may wish to research areas that combine these characteristics. The full ESPC report provides more granular data on the exact locations that performed strongest in Q3 2026.

As always with property investment, thorough research and professional financial advice remain essential before making any commitments. Market conditions can change rapidly, and what performed well in one quarter might not necessarily maintain that performance long-term.

item.title: EYE NEWSFLASH! Government unveils sweeping leasehold reforms as campaigners celebrate and industry backlash erupts
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The government has announced radical reforms to England and Wales' centuries-old leasehold system, marking what ministers describe as the most significant transformation of property ownership in generations. The proposed legislation aims to empower millions of leaseholders while sparking debate across the housing sector.

Key Changes in the Leasehold Reform Bill

The Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill introduces several fundamental changes to property ownership structures. From 2028, ground rents will be capped at £250 annually before gradually reducing to zero over 40 years. The controversial 'marriage value' calculation used in lease extensions will be abolished, potentially making freehold purchases more affordable for existing leaseholders.

Other notable measures include:

  • Stronger protections against excessive administration and permission charges
  • Replacement of forfeiture powers with court-led processes for unpaid charges
  • New powers to cap fees for property alterations or pet ownership
  • Commonhold becoming the default ownership model for new flats

The government estimates these reforms could benefit up to five million leasehold homeowners, with particular focus on addressing what ministers describe as "excessive extraction" from property owners.

Industry Reaction and Potential Impacts

While leasehold campaigners have welcomed the proposals as a long-awaited victory, the reforms have drawn criticism from some property investors and freeholders. Concerns have been raised about the potential impact on existing contracts and pension investments tied to ground rent income streams.

The legislation also extends protections to approximately 1.75 million freehold homeowners on so-called 'fleecehold' estates, where residents pay mandatory maintenance charges. These homeowners will gain new safeguards against aggressive enforcement practices.

Housing minister Matthew Pennycook stated: "The leasehold system denies individuals control over the homes they live in, and have paid for. Our reforms mark the beginning of the end for this feudal system." However, some industry voices warn the changes could create uncertainty in parts of the housing market during the transition period.

As the bill enters Parliament, homeowners may wish to monitor its progress and consider seeking professional advice about how the reforms could affect their property rights and financial commitments. The full impact of these changes will become clearer as the legislation moves through the parliamentary process.

item.title: Santander joins six-times-income mortgage race as buyers offered bigger loans
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Santander has joined the growing number of lenders offering mortgages of up to six times annual income, potentially boosting borrowing power for eligible first-time buyers by up to £90,000. The bank has increased its maximum loan-to-income (LTI) multiple from five to six times earnings for qualifying applicants, provided they meet specific criteria. This move could help buyers struggling to bridge the gap between rising property prices and their incomes, though experts caution that larger loans may lead to higher repayments and could impact housing affordability in certain areas.

What has changed with Santander’s mortgage criteria?

Under the new rules, first-time buyers with a minimum household income of £45,000 and a deposit of at least 10% may now be eligible for mortgages of up to six times their income. For example, a buyer earning £60,000 could potentially borrow £360,000, up from £300,000 under the previous five-times-income limit. Similarly, a household earning £90,000 could see their maximum borrowing increase from £450,000 to £540,000.

The higher multiple also extends to home movers and remortgage customers with individual or joint incomes of at least £100,000. For instance, a household earning £100,000 could now borrow up to £600,000, compared to £550,000 previously. However, all applications remain subject to Santander’s affordability assessments and wider lending criteria.

How does Santander compare to other lenders?

Santander’s decision brings it in line with several major competitors, including Nationwide, Barclays, NatWest, and HSBC, which already offer mortgages of up to six times income under varying eligibility requirements. Aaron Strutt of Trinity Financial noted that Santander risked losing business to rivals offering higher borrowing multiples. He commented: “The lender was already generous, offering up to 5.5 times salary, but not as competitive as some of its peers. This change will likely be welcomed by customers.”

While Santander is somewhat late to adopt this policy, its move reflects a broader trend in the mortgage market. Strutt added: “There is already a surprising number of lenders offering six-times-income mortgages, so Santander’s decision brings it in line with industry standards.”

What should borrowers consider?

Whilst higher borrowing limits can help buyers secure larger mortgages, they also come with potential risks. Larger loans typically mean higher monthly repayments, which could strain household budgets, particularly if interest rates rise. Additionally, increased borrowing power may contribute to upward pressure on house prices in areas where housing supply is limited.

Prospective buyers might wish to carefully assess their financial situation and long-term affordability before opting for a larger mortgage. Consulting an independent mortgage adviser could help ensure that any borrowing aligns with their financial goals and circumstances.

Santander’s move highlights the evolving landscape of mortgage lending, as lenders adapt to meet the needs of buyers in a challenging property market. For those considering a mortgage, staying informed about the latest options and seeking professional advice could be key to making the right decision.

item.title: Charlie Lamdin hits back at estate agents: ‘You’re missing the point’
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The founder of BestAgent, Charlie Lamdin, has responded to criticism from estate agents regarding the platform’s use of property listings, marketing materials, and viewing arrangements. Lamdin emphasised that basic property information will remain on BestAgent, even if agents request the removal of additional content such as photographs and floorplans. His comments come amidst ongoing debates about who controls property marketing material once it is published online.

Debate Over Property Listings

The dispute arose after concerns were raised by Andrew Muskett, manager at David Burr’s Woolpit office in Suffolk, regarding BestAgent’s use of his agency’s marketing material and handling of viewing enquiries. The discussion gained traction following an article in EYE, which sparked further debate among estate agents. Some commentators drew parallels with Houser, a property website that previously faced controversy for its approach to reproducing agents’ listings.

Lamdin defended BestAgent’s practices, stating that basic property information, such as the address, price, size, energy rating, and sold history, is publicly available and not subject to copyright. He argued that agents demanding the removal of listings are “missing the point” and highlighted that fewer than 1% of agents listed on the platform have raised complaints.

Who Controls Marketing Material?

The controversy has reignited questions about the control of property marketing material once it is published online. Lamdin stressed that while agents can request the removal of photographs, floorplans, and descriptions, the underlying property information will remain visible on BestAgent. He also urged agents to consider the implications of removing marketing content, particularly in relation to their obligations to vendors.

Lamdin stated, “Every seller pays their agent to market their home well. An agent who pulls the marketing will need to consider whether that’s in their seller’s best interests, and be ready to explain that choice to their seller.” This statement underscores the potential conflict between agents’ desire to control their marketing material and their duty to act in the best interests of their clients.

The ongoing debate highlights the evolving relationship between estate agents and third-party platforms in the digital age. As the property market continues to adapt to new technologies, the question of who controls online property information remains a contentious issue.

item.title: Misleading property advert lands OnTheMarket and estate agent in trouble with ASA
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) has ruled against property portal OnTheMarket and estate agency Edward Mellor following complaints about a misleading shared ownership property advert. The case highlights the importance of clear pricing information when marketing part-buy, part-rent homes.

Shared ownership details omitted from advert

The disputed listing promoted a two-bedroom semi-detached bungalow with the headline "From £107,500". However, this figure represented only a 50% share of the property, with potential buyers also facing ongoing rent payments, service charges and insurance costs. item.title: Buy-to-let landlords abandon plans to sell as falling flat prices derail exit strategies
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Recent research suggests a notable shift in buy-to-let landlord strategies, with many reconsidering property sales as flat price declines alter their financial calculations. According to estate agency Winkworth's Autumn Prime Outer London Report, fluctuating valuations and changing market conditions have led some landlords to remain in the rental sector rather than exiting as previously planned.

Market fluctuations prompt landlord rethink

Winkworth's data reveals a striking reversal in landlord behaviour between summer and autumn 2023. During the summer months, when the Renters' Rights Act came into force, sales valuations jumped by 18% while lettings valuations dropped by 21%. However, as autumn approached and flat prices softened, some landlords opted to keep properties in the rental market, leading to a 15% annual increase in new lettings instructions across several prime London areas including Clapham, Fulham and St John's Wood.

Mohammad Copley, insights manager at Winkworth, noted: "Our offices' dual focus on sales and lettings provides real-time visibility of landlord decision-making. The changing market dynamics have clearly influenced many investors' strategies."

Regional variations and market impacts

The research uncovered significant regional differences in landlord behaviour. In Clapham and St John's Wood, disappointing sales valuations and strong rental yields have encouraged landlords to retain properties. Meanwhile, areas like Fulham and Parsons Green have seen smaller portfolio owners increasingly opting to sell, often citing growing costs and administrative pressures.

The return of some landlords to the rental market has eased competition among tenants. Whereas summer saw nearly 23 registered tenants competing for each available property, this ratio dropped to around 16 by autumn as supply improved. The report also highlighted a growing divergence between property types, with family homes priced above £1.5 million continuing to attract buyers in several locations, while flats face challenges including higher service charges and building safety concerns.

With further tax changes on the horizon - including increased rental income tax rates from April 2027 - many buy-to-let investors may find themselves regularly reassessing their strategies in response to both market conditions and regulatory shifts.

item.title: Santander joins battle to fix broken property sales process
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

New research reveals that UK property transactions now take an average of 120 days to reach exchange – a 54% increase compared to 2016 figures. With one in four sales collapsing before completion, Santander has joined industry efforts to streamline the process through the National Property Transaction Network (NPTN).

Growing delays in property transactions

Data from Connells Group shows the average time between sale agreement and exchange has extended from 78 days in 2016 to 120 days in 2026. Even market leaders like Connells, whose transactions complete in 110 days on average, face significantly longer timelines than a decade ago. These delays create uncertainty for all parties and increase the risk of transactions falling through.

Chris Rosindale, Chief Operating Officer at Connells Group, commented: "Whilst our performance remains stronger than the market average, today's 110-day timeline still represents an extra month of uncertainty compared to 2016. This clearly demonstrates the need for systemic improvements."

The high cost of failed transactions

Santander's research highlights the financial impact of prolonged sales processes, with their Fixing the Broken Chain report estimating that:

  • 25% of property transactions fail before completion
  • Failed sales cost affected parties an average of £1,240
  • The annual economic impact exceeds £1.5 billion

Lengthy transaction processes account for 19% of collapsed sales, while survey issues contribute to 16% of failures. When deals collapse late in the process – as happens with one in five failed transactions – buyers, sellers and agents face particularly significant setbacks.

Industry collaboration for faster completions

Santander has joined Lloyds Banking Group, Skipton Building Society, Connells Group and technology provider LMS in supporting the NPTN initiative. This collaboration aims to modernise the property transaction process through:

  • Improved communication between parties
  • Standardised documentation
  • Technology-driven solutions

For homeowners considering a move, these industry developments could eventually lead to more reliable transaction timelines. In the current market, allowing additional time for completion and preparing for potential delays might help reduce stress during the moving process.

item.title: Rent arrears behind more than half of landlord repossessions
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent research highlights rent arrears as the primary driver behind landlord repossession actions in the private rental sector, with experts warning that economic pressures could exacerbate the situation for tenants. According to a National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) study, over half of landlords who've sought possession cited unpaid rent as a key factor, raising concerns about the growing financial strain on both tenants and property owners.

Why landlords seek repossession

The NRLA survey, conducted by Pegasus Insight, reveals that 61% of member landlords have initiated repossession proceedings at some point. Among these cases:

  • 53% were primarily due to rent arrears
  • 33% related to tenant anti-social behaviour
  • 26% stemmed from landlords' plans to sell properties

These findings emerge alongside warnings that recent government policies might intensify financial pressures on tenants. The combination of frozen housing benefits and increased taxation on rental income could create a perfect storm, potentially widening the gap between rental costs and what many households can afford.

Budget measures raise concerns

Property experts express particular concern about the impact of the Spring Budget measures. The Office for Budget Responsibility predicts that higher taxes on rental income may lead to increased rents, whilst the ongoing freeze on housing benefit rates threatens to leave more low-income tenants struggling. Research from the Resolution Foundation suggests this shortfall between housing support and actual rents could reach unprecedented levels.

NRLA chief executive Ben Beadle criticised the government's approach: "The Chancellor speaks of helping households with living costs, yet policies like increased taxation on rentals and static housing benefits actively undermine this goal." He warned that without addressing these systemic issues, rent arrears could spiral further, potentially overwhelming local authority housing services.

The situation appears particularly challenging given current economic conditions. With wage growth barely matching inflation and rental supply declining in many areas, affordability pressures show no signs of easing. Letting agents report growing concerns about payment defaults, suggesting landlords may face increasing difficulty maintaining their properties without reliable rental income.

As the private rental sector navigates these challenges, both landlords and tenants might benefit from reviewing their financial arrangements. Those concerned about affordability could explore budgeting support or early communication with landlords about payment difficulties. Meanwhile, property owners affected by rent arrears may wish to seek professional advice about their options whilst remaining mindful of their legal responsibilities towards tenants.

item.title: Property sector ranks second for AI adoption as UK business use doubles
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK property sector has emerged as one of the country's leading industries in artificial intelligence adoption, with nearly half of real estate businesses now using AI tools, according to recent government data analysis. Research conducted by proptech firm Dwelly reveals that 45% of property businesses have implemented AI solutions, ranking the sector second only to information and communication (61%) in technology uptake.

Property Outpaces Finance in AI Adoption

The findings demonstrate significant growth in technology adoption within the real estate industry, which now leads more traditionally tech-focused sectors. Property's 45% adoption rate exceeds that of both financial services and business services, which stand at 39% each. This marks a notable shift in how the property sector approaches digital transformation, though the data doesn't differentiate between different types of real estate businesses.

Across all UK industries, AI usage has doubled in the past year, rising from 16% to 32% of businesses. The research also indicates changing attitudes towards artificial intelligence, with fewer firms considering the technology irrelevant to their operations - down from 51% to 38% over the same period.

From Basic Adoption to Operational Integration

While adoption rates are increasing, experts suggest many businesses are still in the early stages of implementation. Industry professionals note there's a significant difference between occasional administrative use of AI and fully integrating the technology into core business operations.

Sam Humphreys of Dwelly commented: "The real opportunity lies in moving beyond basic adoption and developing technology that can manage entire workflows, improve efficiency and enhance customer experiences." This perspective highlights the potential for more sophisticated applications beyond current implementations.

The research coincides with Dwelly's own expansion strategy, having completed ten acquisitions this year to grow its managed property portfolio to over 15,000 homes. Their approach demonstrates how technology adoption and business growth strategies are becoming increasingly intertwined in the property sector.

As AI becomes more prevalent across industries, the property sector's early adoption positions it well for potential efficiency gains and service improvements. However, the extent to which businesses leverage these technologies beyond basic functions may determine their competitive advantage in an increasingly digital marketplace.

item.title: Three letters that could transform estate agency and end CRM headaches
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A new technological development called Model Context Protocol (MCP) could revolutionise how estate agents and property professionals manage workflows, potentially solving long-standing CRM integration challenges. This innovation acts as a universal translator between different software systems, allowing seamless communication without the need for multiple custom integrations.

How MCP simplifies property management

Traditionally, property professionals have faced significant hurdles when trying to connect various PropTech solutions with their existing CRM systems. Each integration requires custom development, often proving costly and time-consuming. MCP eliminates this complexity by enabling different platforms to communicate directly through AI-powered language models like ChatGPT or Gemini.

For example, when arranging property inspections, users can now simply paste a spreadsheet of properties into their preferred AI interface or issue verbal instructions. The system automatically processes requests and returns confirmations without requiring manual dashboard access. This streamlined approach could save property managers considerable time on routine administrative tasks.

The potential impact on property transactions

Beyond simplifying day-to-day operations, MCP could transform the entire property transaction process. The technology enables different stakeholders – including solicitors, mortgage brokers and surveyors – to communicate more effectively through a standardised protocol. Given that communication breakdowns frequently cause transaction delays, this development might help accelerate the home moving process.

Industry observers note that despite its potential, awareness of MCP remains limited within government and regulatory circles. As the technology becomes more widely adopted, property professionals might wish to explore how it could enhance their service offering and operational efficiency.

Preparing for the MCP revolution

For estate agencies and property management firms considering adopting MCP solutions, the key requirement is having up-to-date software capable of running an MCP server. Early adopters are already demonstrating how the technology can reduce administrative burdens and improve client service.

As PropTech continues to evolve, MCP represents an important step towards creating a more connected, efficient property industry. While the full implications are still emerging, this innovation could fundamentally change how professionals interact with technology throughout the property lifecycle.

With communication being a persistent challenge in property transactions, solutions like MCP might finally provide the tools needed to create a smoother experience for all parties involved in the home moving process.

item.title: OneDome completes major acquisition
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

OneDome has strengthened its position in the mortgage advisory sector by acquiring a majority stake in Cornerstone Finance Group. The deal expands OneDome's combined mortgage distribution network to over 900 advisers, collectively arranging more than £15bn in annual lending. This follows the firm's acquisition of Mortgage Intelligence in 2022, continuing its strategic expansion in the financial services market.

Expanding mortgage advisory capabilities

Cardiff-based Cornerstone Finance Group brings 320 mortgage and protection advisers across 121 appointed representative firms into OneDome's growing network. While financial details remain undisclosed, the arrangement allows Cornerstone to maintain its brand identity, management team and operational independence. The firm will gain access to OneDome's technological platforms, product range and wider distribution channels as part of the agreement.

The acquisition forms part of OneDome's Growth Partners strategy, which supports mortgage brokers with technology solutions, lead generation services and specialist lending options. Advisers within the expanded network may also utilise OneDome's HomeBuyer Service – a fixed-price package combining mortgage advice with conveyancing and transaction support.

Technology-driven brokerage growth

OneDome founder and CEO Babek Ismayil commented on the evolving needs of modern mortgage brokers: "The next generation of successful brokerage businesses will require more than traditional network support. Increasingly, they'll need technological solutions, compelling consumer propositions, capital access and practical growth support alongside broader product offerings."

Cornerstone CEO Haydn Thomas highlighted how the partnership could benefit member firms: "This investment enables accelerated, sustainable growth for Cornerstone. Our advisers gain access to improved pricing through the OneDome network, alongside enhanced lead generation opportunities and greater technological resources."

The Cardiff office will continue as Cornerstone's specialist operational base while expanding its commercial finance activities. The deal reinforces OneDome's ambition to integrate mortgage advice with conveyancing and other property transaction services within a single group structure.

With this acquisition, OneDome solidifies its position as a significant player in the mortgage distribution sector, offering an increasingly comprehensive proposition for both advisers and homebuyers.

item.title: Over-65s hold £2.25tn in property wealth – but few are downsizing
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Homeowners aged 65 and over are sitting on a staggering £2.25tn in property wealth, according to recent research from Savills. This figure marks a dramatic increase compared to three decades ago, when older homeowners held just £232bn in housing equity. The rise reflects decades of house price growth and an ageing population, with older generations now accounting for a significant portion of the UK’s owner-occupied housing wealth. Despite this, relatively few are choosing to downsize, leaving much of this wealth tied up in property.

A Sharp Rise in Housing Wealth

The research highlights the extent to which property wealth has grown among older homeowners. Adjusted for inflation, the £2.25tn held by over-65s represents a 372% increase since 1995 and a 52% rise since 2010. This surge is partly due to the growing number of older homeowners, with households headed by someone aged 65 or over rising from 3.32 million in 1995 to 6.12 million in 2025. Average housing equity has also climbed sharply, increasing from £67,816 in 1995 to £353,539 in 2025.

Lucian Cook, head of residential research at Savills, commented, “The extraordinary increase in housing wealth held by older homeowners reflects three decades of house price growth and a significant demographic shift.” He added that this wealth remains largely concentrated in property until it is released through downsizing, later-life borrowing, or inheritance.

Downsizing Trends and Challenges

Despite the vast sums tied up in property, downsizing remains relatively uncommon among older homeowners. Savills estimates that just 131,200 households downsized during 2025–26, selling properties worth a combined £60.7bn. After purchasing replacement homes, these households released £20.8bn in equity. On average, downsizers sold their properties for £462,500 and bought new homes for £304,150.

Downsizers are more prevalent in higher-value markets, accounting for 33% of sellers disposing of properties worth over £1m. In contrast, they represented just 6.7% of sellers in the £250,000-and-under market. The reluctance to downsize is often driven by a shortage of suitable properties and the financial costs associated with moving, such as stamp duty and legal fees.

Regional Variations in Property Wealth

The South East leads the way in terms of property wealth among older homeowners, with £468bn tied up in housing equity. Around 942,000 households in the region are headed by someone aged 65 or over, reflecting the area’s popularity among retirees and its higher-than-average property values.

While downsizing offers a potential route to releasing equity, many older homeowners appear hesitant to take this step. As a result, much of the UK’s housing wealth remains concentrated in the hands of older generations, with implications for inheritance, later-life borrowing, and the wider property market.

For those considering downsizing, it could be worth exploring the options available, including the availability of suitable properties and the financial implications of moving. With the right planning, downsizing can be a practical way to unlock equity and enhance financial flexibility in later life.

item.title: Courts struggling to cope as possession claims rise
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent figures reveal a significant increase in possession claims across England and Wales, with the private rented sector (PRS) seeing a 21% year-on-year rise. This surge comes amidst growing pressures on the court system and coincides with the impending abolition of Section 21 'no fault' evictions under the Renters Reform Bill.

Court systems under pressure as eviction cases climb

Legal professionals and letting agents report mounting delays in possession cases as courts grapple with higher workloads. The current backlog means some landlords now face waits of several months before cases reach hearing dates, whilst tenants remain in uncertain circumstances during this period.

Several factors may be contributing to this situation:

  • Economic pressures making rent payments more difficult for some tenants
  • Landlords seeking possession before potential changes to eviction rules
  • Increased mortgage costs prompting some landlords to reconsider their portfolios

Section 21 changes on the horizon

The government's proposed Renters Reform Bill, currently progressing through Parliament, will abolish Section 21 notices - the mechanism allowing landlords to regain possession without stating a reason. Whilst intended to improve tenant security, the changes have sparked debate about their potential impact on the rental market.

Industry observers suggest some landlords may be initiating possession proceedings now to avoid navigating the new system later. Others highlight that legitimate grounds for eviction will remain under Section 8 procedures, albeit potentially requiring stronger evidence of tenant breaches.

For those involved in the rental market, it could be worth:

  • Reviewing tenancy agreements to ensure compliance with current regulations
  • Understanding the transitional period as reforms are implemented
  • Seeking professional legal advice regarding possession proceedings

As the proposed reforms continue their legislative journey, all parties in the private rented sector face a period of adjustment. The coming months may see further shifts in possession claim patterns as both landlords and tenants adapt to changing regulations and economic conditions.

item.title: Burnham cracks down on service charges
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Leaseholders in England and Wales are set to benefit from enhanced rights and protections under new government proposals aimed at tackling unfair service charges. The measures, announced by Housing Secretary Andy Burnham, seek to address longstanding concerns about opaque fees and poor management practices in the leasehold sector.

What’s Changing for Leaseholders?

The proposed reforms focus on increasing transparency and fairness in service charges, which cover maintenance, repairs, and other shared costs in leasehold properties. Under the new rules, landlords and managing agents will be required to provide detailed breakdowns of service charges, ensuring leaseholders understand exactly what they are paying for. Additionally, stricter guidelines will be introduced to prevent excessive or unjustified fees.

Leaseholders may also gain the right to challenge service charges more effectively through an independent tribunal. This could provide a stronger avenue for resolving disputes and holding landlords accountable for poor-quality services or unreasonable costs.

Why Are These Reforms Important?

Service charges have long been a contentious issue for leaseholders, with many reporting unclear billing practices and escalating costs. In some cases, homeowners have faced significant financial strain due to unexpected fees or substandard maintenance services. The new measures aim to address these issues by fostering greater accountability and fairness in the leasehold system.

For those considering purchasing a leasehold property, these changes could offer greater peace of mind. Enhanced transparency and stronger rights may make leasehold ownership a more attractive and manageable option for prospective buyers.

What Should Leaseholders Do Next?

Whilst the reforms are yet to be fully implemented, leaseholders may wish to familiarise themselves with their existing rights and responsibilities. Reviewing lease agreements and understanding the breakdown of current service charges could help homeowners identify any potential issues early on.

Borrowers might also consider seeking independent advice if they have concerns about their service charges or the management of their property. Organisations such as the Leasehold Advisory Service (LEASE) can provide valuable guidance and support.

These proposals represent a significant step forward in addressing the challenges faced by leaseholders. By promoting transparency and fairness, the reforms could help create a more balanced and efficient leasehold system for homeowners across the country.

item.title: Room rental hotspots revealed
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The UK’s rental market continues to evolve, with certain areas emerging as hotspots for room rentals due to growing demand and rising prices. Recent data highlights Chesham and Stockport as two locations experiencing significant interest from tenants and landlords alike. These towns are proving to be attractive options for those looking to invest in rental properties or find affordable accommodation.

Chesham: A Growing Rental Hub

Situated in Buckinghamshire, Chesham has seen a surge in demand for room rentals. Its appeal lies in its proximity to London, making it a convenient option for commuters seeking more affordable living arrangements outside the capital. The town’s blend of rural charm and excellent transport links has made it a magnet for tenants, particularly young professionals and students.

Landlords in Chesham are also benefiting from rising rental prices, as competition among tenants drives up costs. For property investors, this could present an opportunity to capitalise on the increasing demand. However, it’s worth noting that whilst rental yields are growing, property prices in the area have also risen, potentially impacting overall returns.

Stockport: A Northern Gem

Stockport, located in Greater Manchester, has also emerged as a key player in the rental market. Known for its affordability and vibrant local economy, the town is attracting tenants who are priced out of nearby Manchester. With a range of amenities, good transport links, and a thriving community, Stockport offers a balanced lifestyle that appeals to a wide demographic.

For landlords, Stockport’s rental market offers promising yields, particularly as demand continues to outstrip supply. The town’s regeneration projects and investment in infrastructure have further boosted its appeal, making it an attractive option for those looking to expand their property portfolios.

What Does This Mean for Renters and Investors?

For tenants, these hotspots represent opportunities to secure affordable accommodation in areas with strong transport links and local amenities. However, rising rents in Chesham and Stockport mean that tenants may need to act quickly to secure the best deals.

For property investors, these locations could offer potential for strong rental yields and capital growth. However, it’s essential to conduct thorough research and consider factors such as property prices, local market conditions, and ongoing costs before making any investment decisions.

As the rental market continues to shift, Chesham and Stockport stand out as areas ripe with potential for both tenants and landlords. Whether seeking affordable accommodation or a promising investment opportunity, these towns are worth keeping an eye on.

item.title: Lettings profitable for eight in ten investors
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

New research suggests that the vast majority of UK landlords are seeing positive returns from their property investments, with a significant proportion achieving substantial profits. The findings highlight the continued appeal of buy-to-let investments, despite recent challenges in the property market.

Strong Returns for Landlords

According to the latest data, an impressive 85% of landlords report making a profit from their lettings. This figure demonstrates the resilience of the buy-to-let sector, even amidst economic uncertainty and rising costs. Notably, 17% of landlords say they are achieving significant returns, indicating that well-managed property investments can still yield strong financial rewards.

Factors Influencing Profitability

Several factors may contribute to the profitability of buy-to-let investments. Location remains a key consideration, with properties in high-demand areas often commanding higher rental yields. Careful property selection, effective tenant management, and strategic financing decisions can also play a crucial role in maximising returns.

Landlords might also consider the potential benefits of longer-term tenancies, which can reduce void periods and associated costs. Additionally, maintaining properties to a high standard could help attract and retain quality tenants, further supporting profitability.

Challenges and Considerations

While the research paints a positive picture for many landlords, it’s important to acknowledge the challenges facing the sector. Rising interest rates, increased regulation, and higher maintenance costs have put pressure on some investors. Those considering entering the buy-to-let market may wish to carefully assess their financial position and seek professional advice to ensure they are well-prepared for potential hurdles.

Despite these challenges, the findings suggest that, for many, property investment remains a viable and potentially lucrative option. With careful planning and management, landlords could continue to achieve strong returns in the lettings market.

As with any investment, thorough research and a clear understanding of the risks and rewards are essential. Landlords and potential investors might find it valuable to stay informed about market trends and seek expert guidance to make well-informed decisions.
